strengths: Broad and thorough empirical coverage: 33 model organisms across 4 families (SDF, emergent misalignment, subliminal learning, taboo) and 7 models spanning 1B–32B parameters and 3 architectures, with per-organism breakdowns in the appendix.

The interpretability-agent evaluation is a genuinely useful methodological contribution: it provides a reproducible, quantitative ground truth for assessing model-diffing informativeness and mitigates researcher bias in interpreting activation differences.

The causal ablation analysis (Section 5, projecting out the difference direction and measuring CE loss on finetuning vs. pretraining data) goes beyond correlational evidence and supports the overfitting hypothesis, including honest reporting of the disconfirming Gemma3 1B result.

Strong ablations and controls throughout: position/layer sweeps, base-vs-chat diffing, full vs. LoRA finetuning, data-mixing mitigation, CAFT mitigation, domain-adapted VL models as a 'more realistic' test case, multiple agent LLMs, and a Bayesian hierarchical GLM for the aggregate statistics.

Clear, safety-relevant message: narrow-finetuned model organisms may be poor proxies for broad post-training, with actionable implications (mixing pretraining data) and honest discussion of trade-offs (FFA score degradation).
weaknesses: The core phenomenon—that activation differences between base and finetuned models encode finetuning-related signal—is fairly intuitive and consistent with prior model-diffing work (crosscoders, persona vectors, logit-lens analyses); the main novelty lies in systematic quantification and the agent-based evaluation rather than a fundamentally new insight.

Heavy and somewhat circular reliance on LLM graders: the same family of grader models (gpt-5-mini/nano) defines 'token relevance,' selects Patchscope scaling factors, judges coherence, and grades agent hypotheses against rubrics. This introduces potential bias toward methods whose outputs are easy for LLM graders to parse, and the paper's headline numbers (e.g., '30x better at specific details') depend entirely on grader behavior.

Evaluation of the phenomenon is concentrated on extremely mono-semantic, often synthetic finetuning corpora; the paper's own Domain-organism results (D.5) show the bias is nearly absent for more realistic domain finetuning, which somewhat undercuts the breadth implied by the title and abstract. Only one subliminal organism is tested, and one SDF organism is excluded from main results for inflating relevance scores, raising mild cherry-picking concerns.

Reproducibility statement is incomplete: the appendix states 'All code is available at' with no URL, which is a significant gap for a paper whose central selling point is a reproducible automated evaluation pipeline. The pipeline itself (binary search with grader feedback, grader-based scaling-factor tournaments, agent interaction budgets) is complex and has many unvalidated hyperparameters.

The grading rubrics (e.g., for SDF) emphasize surface-level matching of key facts and tokens, so 'token relevance' and agent grades may measure lexical overlap rather than deeper understanding of the finetuning objective; human validation of grader judgments is not reported.

Claims in the abstract/introduction ('cannot be sure that there are no further issues', warnings about model organisms) are appropriately hedged, but the mechanistic explanation remains speculative (the paper itself acknowledges this), and the mitigation (data mixing) is only demonstrated for SDF and one EM setting with noted model-specific inconsistencies.

strengths: Broad empirical scope: the study covers 33 model organisms from 4 families (SDF, emergent misalignment, subliminal learning, Taboo) across 7 model architectures and scales (1B–32B), giving reasonable evidence that the phenomenon is not idiosyncratic to one setting.

The interpretability-agent evaluation methodology is a thoughtful attempt to quantify model-diffing informativeness with ground-truth rubrics, reducing researcher subjectivity in interpreting activation differences.

Causal analysis (Eq. 1–2, projection ablations) supports the overfitting hypothesis, and the mitigation experiments (data mixing, reduced training samples, CAFT) add practical value, including honest reporting of trade-offs (e.g., FFA scores decline with mixing).

Honest reporting of negative/limiting results: Gemma3 1B's causal effect is positive on pretraining data, the bias is much weaker on realistic domain-finetuned VLMs, and agent variance/heavy tails are disclosed.
Extensive appendices with detailed prompts, rubrics, and per-organism results improve transparency of the pipeline.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on LLM graders throughout the pipeline (gpt-5-mini for token relevance and hypothesis grading, gpt-5-nano for coherence, grader-selected Patchscope scaling factors) introduces potential circularity and unquantified bias; the token-relevance grader is explicitly acknowledged as a noise source (footnote 9, exclusion of IGNORE COMMENT), yet it underpins headline quantitative claims.

The core observation is arguably expected: activation differences between base and narrowly finetuned models on homogeneous data will encode the finetuning domain; steering with mean difference vectors producing finetune-like text is a relatively straightforward application of existing steering/Patchscope techniques rather than a conceptual advance.

Several experimental cells are thin: only one Subliminal organism (n=1) supports claims about that family; blackbox baselines may be under-provisioned relative to the ADL agent, making the '2x/30x better' comparisons somewhat constructed (agents with richer privileged information vs. limited chat access).

The 'why' analysis is incomplete and internally mixed: the overfitting explanation fails for Gemma3 1B (positive causal effect on pretraining data), and the mechanism discussion remains largely conjectural, as acknowledged in the limitations.
Reproducibility statement is incomplete: Section A says 'All code is available at' with no URL or repository provided, which undermines the paper's claim of a 'fully reproducible methodology'.

The claimed significance for AI safety rests on an inference chain (model organisms are proxies; traces make them unrealistic proxies) that is plausible but not directly demonstrated for any consequential downstream study; the middle-layer choice (ℓ = ⌊L/2⌋) is not justified or ablated across layers.

strengths: Timely and practically relevant question: whether narrowly finetuned 'model organisms' (widely used in AI safety/interpretability research) carry detectable artifacts that compromise their validity as proxies for broader finetuning.

Breadth of empirical evidence: 33 model organisms across 4 organism families (SDF, emergent misalignment, subliminal learning, taboo), 7 models from 1B to 32B parameters and multiple architectures (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen), which substantially strengthens the generality of the central claim.

Novel and well-motivated evaluation methodology: the LLM-based interpretability agent with ADL access vs. blackbox-only baselines provides a quantitative, reproducible ground truth for assessing model-diffing informativeness, reducing researcher bias in interpreting activation differences. The statistical treatment (Bayesian hierarchical GLM with HiBayes, 5 reruns per configuration, HDI analysis) is unusually rigorous for interpretability work.

Causal analysis goes beyond correlation: the projection-based ablation (Eq. 1-2) establishes that the detected bias is causally beneficial for modeling the finetuning data and (for two of three models) harmful for pretraining data, supporting the overfitting hypothesis.

Practical mitigation study with an honest trade-off analysis (mixing pretraining data reduces bias but also reduces false-fact internalization), plus additional ablations (full vs. LoRA finetuning, CAFT, reduced training samples) in the appendix.

Good tests of robustness: comparing base-to-finetuned-chat (Section 4.2) shows the effect survives the base-to-chat transformation; the domain-adapted VLM experiments (D.5) honestly report where the phenomenon weakens.
Extensive appendix with prompts, rubrics, and qualitative examples supports transparency of the evaluation pipeline.
weaknesses: Heavy dependence on LLM-as-judge throughout (graders, coherence checks, Patchscope scale selection, agent grading). The paper itself acknowledges grader noise, but the pipeline has multiple circularity risks: e.g., the token-relevance grader is given the top-100 frequent tokens of the finetuning dataset, which could partially leak finetuning information into the 'relevance' metric; the Patchscope scaling factor is selected by maximizing 'semantically coherent tokens,' embedding an LLM prior into what is presented as an objective measurement.

The interpretability agent comparison may be somewhat confounded: the ADL agent's system prompt explicitly tells it that 'activation differences on the first few tokens often carry finetune-specific signal' and how to interpret ADL results, while the headline statistics (e.g., '30x better at specific details') are based on LLM-graded 1-5 scores with a single grader model; grader-agent (GPT-5 family) shared biases are not fully addressed.

Incomplete reproducibility statement: Section A ('All code is available at') is empty/truncated in the submitted manuscript, and the setup depends on proprietary models (gpt-5, gpt-5-mini, gpt-5-nano, Gemini) hosted via third parties, which weakens reproducibility claims.

Asymmetric organism coverage: only one Subliminal organism (single model, single object) and relatively few Taboo organisms; the strong blackbox performance on Taboo suggests results are sensitive to organism type, and the central narrative would benefit from more balanced coverage.

Mechanistic understanding remains shallow: the overfitting explanation is supported for SDF organisms but the causal analysis covers only three small models and only SDF; the Gemma3 1B anomaly (positive causal effect on pretraining data) is explained only speculatively.

The core observation that finetuning leaves traces in activation differences on out-of-domain inputs is somewhat anticipated by prior model-diffing work (crosscoders, logit difference amplification); the novelty lies mainly in the early-token/simple-average framing and the agent-based evaluation, so positioning relative to these concurrent works could be sharper.

Some claims in the abstract/intro are stronger than the evidence (e.g., 'cannot be sure that there are no further issues'; the generalization to realistic post-training remains an extrapolation given that the one realistic domain-finetuning test showed the bias 'almost entirely absent').
